7.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask a hip patient?"
- "Pain, limp, stiffness, deformity, snapping and function."
- "Function = the Oxford Hip Score items: walking, stairs, socks, car."
- "Then past history: childhood hip disease, injections, steroids, operations."

### Pain — where and when
| Site | Think of |
|---|---|
| Groin, 1 inch below and lateral to the femoral pulse | the hip joint |
| Lateral thigh | trochanteric bursitis |
| Buttock | referred from the spine |
| Knee | referred from the hip (obturator nerve) |

- **C sign** (hand cupping the hip) → intra-articular problem (Exam Techniques)
- First question: intra- or extra-articular? Hip or referred?

[[FIG: Fig 7.1 — Pain referred from the spine; hip pain felt in the knee · 7.01

### Function, limp, stiffness, snapping
- Function = **Oxford Hip Score** items: walking, support, stairs, socks, toenails, car (Kasr Al-Ainy)

| Complaint | Causes |
|---|---|
| Limp | pain, LLD, weak abductors, instability |
| Stiffness | RA, AS or SLE |
| Snapping | external ITB, internal iliopsoas, labrum or loose body |

- **Memory:** four limp causes; three snaps — outside, inside, in the joint
- LLD = leg length discrepancy; RA = rheumatoid arthritis; AS = ankylosing spondylitis
- SLE = systemic lupus; ITB = iliotibial band

### Personal and past history
| Clue | Points to |
|---|---|
| Neonate | septic arthritis, DDH |
| 6–10 years | Perthes disease |
| 12–14 years | SUFE |
| Adolescent, athlete | snapping hip, FAI, labral tear |
| Elderly | OA, AVN, fracture |
| Steroids, alcohol | AVN |

- DDH = developmental dysplasia of the hip; SUFE = slipped upper femoral epiphysis
- FAI = femoroacetabular impingement; OA = osteoarthritis; AVN = avascular necrosis
- **Memory:** newborn DDH, child Perthes, teenager SUFE, elderly OA

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Pain | where? After activity or at night? |
| Function | walking, stairs, socks, car (Oxford Hip Score) |
| Past | childhood hip, surgery, injections |
| Spine | previous spine surgery? It changes the plan |

- **Red flags:** pain at night → infection or tumour
- General interview and pain analysis → ch 1

7.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this hip"
- "Standing: look, walk, pelvic level, blocks, Trendelenburg."
- "Supine: square, lengths, feel, Thomas, move, special tests."
- "Side, prone, sitting; then neurovascular, spine, knee and groin."

- **Whole hip exam (video):** [▶ Oxford Medical Education · 9:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTfDvFCPZ_w)

### The route on one page
| Position | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| Standing | Look: clues — aid, appliance, shoe raise |
| Walking | Gait: antalgic, Trendelenburg, short-limb, gluteus maximus |
| Standing | Look front, side, behind (DCS); pelvic level, blocks; Trendelenburg |
| Supine | Square the pelvis; apparent and true length, Galeazzi, Bryant |
| Supine | Feel landmarks, pulse over the head; Thomas first, then range |
| Supine | Special: FADIR, FABER, log roll, Stinchfield, telescoping, snapping |
| Side-lying, prone | GT, abductor power, Nélaton, Ober, piriformis; extension, Craig, Ely, Phelps |
| Sitting → Finish | iliopsoas power, Tripod; neuro, vascular, spine, SIJ, knee, groin |

- **Memory:** Look, Feel, Move, Measure, Special · then Neuro, Vascular, Joints above/below

### Standing and walking
#### Clues and gait
| Step | Do |
|---|---|
| Clues | walking aid, appliance, shoe or heel raise |
| Walk | up and back three times; front, side, behind |

- The stick is held in the **opposite** hand → less abductor force (Nagah)

[[FIG: Fig 7.2 — Walking stick as a clue · 7.02

- **Coxalgic** gait: trunk leans over the hip, pelvis stays level; others → ch 1 (1.3)
- **Memory:** dip = short limb; lurch = unstable hip

#### Look — front, side, behind, other side
| View | Look for |
|---|---|
| Front | ASIS levels, attitude, patella, quadriceps wasting |
| Side | lordosis (hides a fixed flexion deformity, FFD), knee flexion |
| Behind | scoliosis, gluteal wasting, creases, scars |

- ASIS = anterior superior iliac spine
- Say "**attitude**", not deformity, until examined (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Memory:** at every view think **DCS** — deformity, contour and wasting, skin

[[FIG: Fig 7.3 — Look from front, side and behind · 7.02

#### Measure — pelvic level
- Stance: feet flat, knees straight; are both ASIS level?
- Pelvis tilted → blocks under the short leg (7.3)
- Then Trendelenburg (7.4), sound side first

### Supine
#### Look — square the pelvis
- **Square the pelvis**: ASIS line at right angles to the couch edge
- Cannot square → fixed adduction or abduction deformity
- Then lengths (7.3), before Thomas

[[FIG: Fig 7.4 — Squaring the pelvis on the couch · 7.02

#### Feel
- Feel is the most forgotten step (Kasr Al-Ainy); landmarks: ASIS, inguinal ligament, greater trochanter (GT), ischial tuberosity
- Slide up from below; the first bone you hit is the landmark

| Feel | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Below inguinal ligament, lateral to the artery | femoral head |
| No femoral pulse over the head | head dislocated |
| Warmth, nodes, tenderness | infection or inflammation |

[[FIG: Fig 7.5 — Femoral pulse at the mid-inguinal point · 7.02

#### Move
- Thomas test first: FFD and flexion range together
- Active, then passive; "painfully limited" is not "limited"
- Fix the pelvis: hand on both ASIS, or other leg over the couch edge

| Movement (Nagah) | Normal |
|---|---|
| Flexion | 120–135° |
| Extension | 0–30° |
| Abduction | 0–45° |
| Adduction | 0–30° |
| Internal / external rotation | 30° / 45° |

- Rotation in extension and in 90° flexion; read the patella
- **Memory:** abduction and external rotation 45°; adduction and internal rotation 30°
- Abduction short of neutral → abduction deformity, not "adduction 20°" (Kasr Al-Ainy)

[[FIG: Fig 7.6 — Flexion with the knee bent · 7.02
[[FIG: Fig 7.7 — Abduction with the pelvis fixed · 7.02
[[FIG: Fig 7.8 — Rotation in extension and in flexion · 7.02

### Side-lying, prone, sitting
| Position | Do |
|---|---|
| Side-lying | GT tenderness, abductor power (MRC grade 0–5), Ober, piriformis |
| Prone | extension, rotation, Craig, Ely, Phelps |
| Sitting | iliopsoas power, tripod sign |

- MRC = Medical Research Council grade

[[FIG: Fig 7.9 — Side-lying: trochanter and abductor power · 7.02
[[FIG: Fig 7.10 — Extension tested prone · 7.02

### Finish
- Pulses; femoral, sciatic and lateral femoral cutaneous nerves
- "I would examine the spine, sacroiliac joint (SIJ), knee and groin"

PITFALL — "turning a patient with a big FFD prone"
- Severe pain, the spine compensates, and the station is lost (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Say → "**I would avoid lying the patient prone; I test extension side-lying.**"

7.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you assess this shortening?"
- "Apparent or true? True: tibial or femoral? Femoral: above or below the trochanter?"
- "Apparent: xiphisternum to medial malleolus. True: ASIS to medial malleolus."

- **Memory:** three questions, three tests: tape, Galeazzi, Bryant

### Apparent versus true
| | Apparent | True |
|---|---|---|
| From | xiphisternum (or umbilicus) | ASIS |
| To | medial malleolus | medial malleolus |
| Pelvis | as it lies | squared, sound leg matched |
| Means | deformity or tilt | the bone is short |

- Adduction → leg looks short; abduction → looks long
- Each 10° fixed adduction adds about 3 cm apparent shortening (Exam Techniques)

[[FIG: Fig 7.11 — Adduction attitude levelled by a block · 7.03
[[FIG: Fig 7.12 — Apparent length from the xiphisternum · 7.03
[[FIG: Fig 7.13 — True length from the ASIS · 7.03

#### Measuring well
- Hook the tape under the ASIS; take the malleolus from below
- A wrong point alone gives about 1 cm error (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Fixed deformity → put the sound leg in the same position first

[[FIG: Fig 7.14 — Sound leg adducted to match · 7.03
[[FIG: Fig 7.15 — Apparent difference, true lengths equal · 7.03

#### Segmental measurement
- Use it when a knee deformity cannot be matched
- Femur: GT tip to knee joint line; tibia: joint line to malleolus

[[FIG: Fig 7.16 — Femoral segment: GT tip to lateral joint line · 7.03

### Where does the pelvic tilt come from?
| Level | Cause |
|---|---|
| Spine | scoliosis |
| Pelvis | malunited fracture |
| Hip | adduction or abduction deformity |
| Knee | knee FFD |

- **Memory:** search top to bottom — spine, pelvis, hip, knee

#### Block test
- **Aim:** LLD standing, apart from fixed pelvic tilt
- **How:** blocks under the short leg until the ASIS are level
- **Positive:** pelvis levels → LLD = block height; stays tilted → spine cause
- **Why:** the patient feels level; it includes the foot (Exam Techniques)
- **Trap:** a level pelvis may hide symmetrical bilateral deformity
- **Video:** [▶ Abuja Orthopedics · 2:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cPHU9zDxfsc)

[[FIG: Fig 7.17 — Blocks until the pelvis is level · 7.03

#### Galeazzi test
- **Aim:** is true shortening in the femur or the tibia?
- **How:** supine, knees bent; set the heels together and level
- **Positive:** knee behind (side view) → femoral; knee lower (front) → tibial
- **Why:** the shorter segment shows at the knee
- **Video:** [▶ American Family Physician · 1:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=C86RsR_E6_I)

[[FIG: Fig 7.18 — Galeazzi test: heels together, knees bent · 7.03

### Is the shortening above the trochanter?
- **Memory:** neck (coxa vara, fracture, SUFE), head (Perthes), out of the socket (dislocation)
- GT rides up → slack abductors → Trendelenburg positive

[[FIG: Fig 7.19 — Causes of shortening above the trochanter · 7.03

#### Bryant's triangle
- **Aim:** shortening above the trochanter, one side
- **How:** supine; thumb on ASIS, finger on GT tip; compare vertical gaps
- **Positive:** shorter gap on the affected side → supratrochanteric
- **Why:** the GT has moved up toward the iliac crest
- **Trap:** useless when both hips are affected
- **Video:** [▶ eConceptual (Prof Anil Dhal) · 1:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3ES5anqHRqs)

[[FIG: Fig 7.20 — Bryant's triangle: course slide and patient · 7.03

#### Nélaton's line
- **Aim:** shortening above the trochanter
- **How:** side-lying; draw a line from ASIS to ischial tuberosity
- **Positive:** GT tip above the line → supratrochanteric (normal: on or below)
- **Video:** [▶ Ryan Duffy · 0:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mAcJgPeB1Jk)

[[FIG: Fig 7.21 — Nélaton's line from ASIS to ischial tuberosity · 7.03

#### Other lines
| Line | Normal | Abnormal |
|---|---|---|
| Schoemaker (GT through ASIS, both sides) | meet above the umbilicus | off midline → one side; below → both |

### Measuring the deformity
| Deformity | How |
|---|---|
| Flexion | Thomas test; or Milch pelvifemoral angle, normal 50° (Nagah) |
| Adduction / abduction | limb to ASIS line: <90° adduction, >90° abduction |
| Rotation | patella direction; Craig test for anteversion |

PITFALL — "Bryant's triangle is equal, so no shortening"
- Equal triangles may mean both hips are short, e.g. bilateral DDH
- Say → "**Bryant's compares sides; for bilateral cases I use Schoemaker's line.**"

7.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "the two T's of the hip"
- "Trendelenburg standing and Thomas supine — a must in every hip exam (Kasr Al-Ainy)."
- "Then pain tests (FADIR, FABER, log roll) and tightness tests (Ober, Ely)."

### Is the abductor working?
#### Trendelenburg test
- **Aim:** abductor mechanism of the standing hip
- **How:** patient stands on the test leg, bends the other knee, holds 30 s
- **Positive:** lifted side drops, or cannot hold 30 s → abductors fail
- **Why:** weak abductors cannot hold the pelvis level
- **Trap:** test the sound side first; trunk lean hides the drop (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yQ7fg1GN4Tw)

[[FIG: Fig 7.22 — Positive Trendelenburg: the lifted side drops · 7.04

| Positive because (Nagah) | Example |
|---|---|
| Power | weak abductors, superior gluteal nerve, L5 root |
| Fulcrum | dislocation, DDH |
| Lever | coxa vara, short neck, non-union |
| Pain | OA, AVN |

HIGH YIELD — Memory hook
- Four causes: **Power, Fulcrum, Lever, Pain**

- False negative: arthrodesis or ankylosed hip
- Invalid: poor balance, severe weakness, under age 4 (McRae)

[[FIG: Fig 7.23 — Four causes: weakness, pain, coxa vara, DDH · 7.04

### Is there a hidden deformity?
#### Thomas test
- **Aim:** hidden fixed flexion deformity of the hip
- **How:** other hip held fully flexed; your hand under the lumbar spine
- **Positive:** tested thigh rises off the couch → FFD = the angle
- **Why:** lordosis masks up to 30° FFD (Exam Techniques)
- **Trap:** knee FFD → hang the leg over the couch edge; never after THR
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel (original Thomas) · 0:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HPBYjiUMikw)

[[FIG: Fig 7.24 — Thomas test: hand under the back, other hip held · 7.04
[[FIG: Fig 7.25 — Knee FFD removed over the couch edge · 7.04

### Is the pain from the joint?
- **Memory:** the name is the movement — FADIR = flexion, adduction, internal rotation; FABER = flexion, abduction, external rotation

#### FADIR (anterior impingement) test
- **Aim:** anterosuperior labral tear or FAI
- **How:** supine; flex to 90°, adduct, internally rotate
- **Positive:** groin pain, sometimes a click → labral tear or FAI
- **Why:** femoral neck closes on the anterosuperior rim
- **Trap:** sensitive, not specific; needs a normal range first (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xyJUIhsL4lg)

[[FIG: Fig 7.26 — FADIR: flexion, adduction, internal rotation · 7.04

| Repeat FADIR | Squeeze | Distraction |
|---|---|---|
| Labral tear | painful | painless |
| Bone (e.g. AVN) | painful | painful |

- **Memory:** labrum hurts on squeeze only; bone hurts both ways

#### FABER (Patrick) test
- **Aim:** hip or SIJ pain
- **How:** supine, figure-4; fix the opposite ASIS, press the knee down
- **Positive:** pain, or knee stays higher → hip or SIJ
- **Why:** groin pain → hip; back pain → SIJ (Nagah)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=89Qiht82zmg)

[[FIG: Fig 7.27 — FABER: figure-4, opposite ASIS fixed · 7.04

#### Posterior impingement test
- **Aim:** posterior rim against the femoral neck
- **How:** at the couch edge, other hip flexed; extend, abduct, externally rotate
- **Positive:** deep posterior hip pain → posterior impingement
- **Why:** squeezes the posterior labrum
- **Video:** [▶ The Physio Channel · 0:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qobPzFnhRY0)

[[FIG: Fig 7.28 — Posterior impingement test at the couch edge · 7.04

#### Log roll test
- **Aim:** intra-articular hip pain; capsular laxity
- **How:** supine, leg straight; roll it gently in and out
- **Positive:** pain → intra-articular; more external roll, no end point → laxity
- **Why:** moves only the head in the socket — specific for the hip
- **Video:** [▶ Sports Med Review · 0:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_k5FUEg_F50)

#### Hip quadrant (scour) test
- **Aim:** joint surface or labrum as the pain source
- **How:** hip flexed 90°; push down through the knee, sweep an arc
- **Positive:** pain, click or grinding → labrum, arthritis or AVN
- **Why:** pressure down the femur loads the joint through the arc
- **Video:** [▶ Educom Continuing Education · 1:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tsCKRDDv4ss)

#### Stinchfield test
- **Aim:** hip joint pathology
- **How:** patient raises the straight leg to 45°; you resist
- **Positive:** groin pain → hip disease; cannot lift after a fall → neck fracture
- **Why:** iliopsoas loads the joint, about twice body weight (Reider)

### Is a muscle tight?
- **Memory:** one test per side of the thigh — Ober lateral, Ely front, Phelps medial, Tripod back

#### Ober test
- **Aim:** ITB or tensor fascia lata contracture
- **How:** sound side down; abduct and extend the upper hip, knee bent; lower it
- **Positive:** leg stays abducted → tight ITB
- **Why:** a tight band cannot let the hip adduct past midline
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Amjv6FzDeLE)

[[FIG: Fig 7.31 — Ober test, affected side up · 7.04

#### Ely test
- **Aim:** rectus femoris contracture
- **How:** prone; flex the knee passively
- **Positive:** buttock on that side rises → tight rectus femoris
- **Why:** rectus crosses hip and knee; the hip flexes to relieve it
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0FgacndWb4Q)

[[FIG: Fig 7.32 — Ely test: buttock rises with knee flexion · 7.04

#### Phelps test
- **Aim:** gracilis contracture
- **How:** prone; abduct both straight legs fully, then bend the knees
- **Positive:** more abduction once the knees bend → tight gracilis
- **Why:** knee flexion slackens gracilis, which crosses the knee
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NDsPj1qATiU)

[[FIG: Fig 7.33 — Phelps test: abduction gained with knees bent · 7.04

#### Tripod sign
- **Aim:** hamstring contracture
- **How:** sitting, knees at 90°; extend one knee passively
- **Positive:** falls back onto the hands → tight hamstrings
- **Why:** tight hamstrings extend the hip; exclude sciatic tension
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mRab9U81HSU)

### Is a muscle weak or irritated?
#### Piriformis (FAIR) test
- **Aim:** piriformis tendinitis or piriformis syndrome
- **How:** sound side down, hip 45°, knee 90°; push the knee down
- **Positive:** local pain → tendinitis; pain down the leg → syndrome (Nagah)
- **Why:** the stretch pulls piriformis over the sciatic nerve

- **Aim:** hip flexor power, femoral nerve L2–L4
- **How:** sitting at the couch edge, patient lifts the thigh; you resist
- **Positive:** weak or painful flexion → iliopsoas or femoral nerve

### Is the femur twisted?
#### Craig test
- **Aim:** femoral anteversion
- **How:** prone, knee 90°; rotate the leg until the GT is most lateral
- **Positive:** tibia-to-vertical angle above normal 8–15° → more anteversion (Reider)

### Is the hip unstable or snapping?
#### Telescoping
- **Aim:** unstable, dislocated hip
- **How:** supine; steady the pelvis, push and pull along the femur
- **Positive:** piston movement, more than the sound side → unstable
- **Why:** head not held: DDH, septic sequel, paralytic, non-union

#### Iliopsoas snapping test
- **Aim:** internal snapping hip
- **How:** supine; take the hip from flexion-abduction-external rotation into extension

#### Trendelenburg test
- **Aim:** abductor mechanism of the standing hip
- **How:** patient stands on the test leg, bends the other knee, holds 30 s
- **Positive:** lifted side drops, or cannot hold 30 s → abductors fail
- **Why:** weak abductors cannot hold the pelvis level
- **Trap:** test the sound side first; trunk lean hides the drop (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yQ7fg1GN4Tw)

|---|---|
| Power | weak abductors, superior gluteal nerve, L5 root |
| Fulcrum | dislocation, DDH |
| Lever | coxa vara, short neck, non-union |
| Pain | OA, AVN |

- Four causes: **Power, Fulcrum, Lever, Pain**

- False negative: arthrodesis or ankylosed hip

7.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "two-minute short case"
- "Spot: gait, aid, attitude, scar. Do: length, Thomas, rotation, Trendelenburg."
- "Say: one diagnosis and one differential."

### Osteoarthritis of the hip
- **Spot:** older patient, stick, antalgic gait, flexion-adduction-external rotation
- **Do:** Thomas, apparent vs true length, painful rotation, Trendelenburg
- **Say:** "OA right hip, fixed flexion and adduction. Differential: AVN."

[[FIG: Fig 7.40 — OA: joint-space loss; course patient with a stick · 7.05

### Ankylosed (fused) hip
- **Spot:** stiff hip, pelvis and spine move instead, extra lordosis
- **Do:** solidity: guarding on sudden movement
- **Do:** position in three planes, true length; Trendelenburg falsely negative
- **Say:** "Ankylosed left hip in fixed flexion. Differential: severe OA stiffness."

[[FIG: Fig 7.41 — Fused-hip gait; testing a fusion for solidity · 7.05

### Neglected DDH in the adult
- **Spot:** short leg, Trendelenburg gait (waddling if bilateral), lordosis
- **Do:** telescoping, supratrochanteric shortening, pulse over an empty socket
- **Do:** spine; back pain, OA of the false joint
- **Say:** "Neglected DDH, high dislocation. Differential: septic hip sequel."

[[FIG: Fig 7.42 — Untreated dislocated left hip, young adult · 7.05

### Total hip replacement (well or failed)
- **Spot:** scar (anterior, lateral or posterior), aid, gait
- **Do:** length, Trendelenburg, gentle range; no Thomas test
- **Do:** pain on movement → loosening or infection; sinus → infection
- **Say:** "Right THR, failing with pain. Differential: loosening vs infection."

[[FIG: Fig 7.43 — Cemented THR; trochanteric wires on X-ray · 7.05

### Excision arthroplasty (Girdlestone)
- **Spot:** short leg, crutches, old hip scar; after infected or failed THR
- **Do:** true length and telescoping — marked shortening, femur rides up (Campbell)
- **Do:** a sinus → infection not yet controlled
- **Say:** "Right Girdlestone after infected THR. Differential: neglected DDH."

[[FIG: Fig 7.48 — Infected THR, then excision arthroplasty · 7.05

### Avascular necrosis
- **Spot:** young adult, limp; ask steroids, alcohol, sickle cell (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Do:** other joints — sickle cell and steroids are systemic
- **Do:** FADIR painful with squeeze and with distraction → bony source
- **Say:** "AVN right femoral head. Differential: early OA."

[[FIG: Fig 7.44 — Collapsed head; crescent sign · 7.05

### Perthes or SUFE in the adult
- **Spot:** young adult, short leg, limp
- **Do:** Perthes: restricted rotation; SUFE: lost internal rotation and abduction
- **Do:** hip rolls into external rotation as you flex it → SUFE
- **Say:** "Post-Perthes deformed head, early OA. Differential: SUFE sequel."

### Differential of a painful stiff hip
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| Traumatic | old fracture, AVN after fracture |
| Inflammatory | RA, crystal disease, infection |
| Neoplastic | PVNS, synovial chondromatosis, metastasis |
| Degenerative | primary or secondary OA |
| Referred | lumbar spine — commonest |

### OSCE cards in one table
| Test | Position | Positive means |
|---|---|---|
| Block test | Standing | pelvis levels → LLD = block height |
| Galeazzi test | Supine | knee behind → femoral; knee lower → tibial |
| Bryant's triangle | Supine | shorter ASIS–GT gap → supratrochanteric |
| Nélaton's line | Side-lying | GT tip above the line → supratrochanteric |
| Trendelenburg test | Standing | lifted side drops → abductors fail |
| Thomas test | Supine | thigh rises → FFD = the angle |
| FADIR | Supine | groin pain → labral tear or FAI |
